title: Power for the most remote place
statement: Space, where maintenance is impossible and energy autonomy is not optional.
facts: IY1EH5 Engineering Global Challenge, University of Hull

chapters.kicker: Energy Harvesting for Remote Sensor Networks
chapters.title: Power for the *most remote* place
chapters.text: My concept for the group brief: a satellite that makes its own electricity from sunlight, with no moving parts and no fuel. Scroll to follow the energy.

chapters.title: *1361* watts on every square metre
chapters.text: Above the atmosphere, nothing filters the Sun. That is the total solar irradiance in low Earth orbit (Kopp and Lean, 2011), and the whole system is built to catch it.

chapters.title: A dish that *bends light* to one point
chapters.text: A revolved parabola sends every ray parallel to its axis to the same focal point. Three struts hold a collar right at the focus.

chapters.title: Copper at the *hot spot*
chapters.text: A hollow copper tube sits in the collar and soaks up the concentrated flux. Copper conducts heat away fast, so the energy moves instead of pooling.

chapters.title: Heat, carried *through the body*
chapters.text: Copper heat pipes run from the receiver, through the mounting, into the satellite and across to the shadow-facing side.

chapters.title: Temperature difference *becomes voltage*
chapters.text: A copper spreader evens out the heat across a bismuth telluride TEG. The difference between its hot and cold faces pushes charge through the semiconductor: the Seebeck effect.

chapters.title: Facing the *cold of deep space*
chapters.text: With no air in orbit, waste heat can only leave as radiation. The radiator sits flush in a recess on the shadow side, and six fins multiply its radiating area.

chapters.title: A satellite that *powers itself*
chapters.text: A boost converter conditions the output into a battery module, and a sensor transmits to ground stations during line-of-sight windows. Everything lives in one aluminium shell.

calc.title: Run the *numbers*
calc.intro: The same first-order relationships from the report. The design point is a 200 mm dish and a 100 K difference across the TEG.
calc.note: Open-circuit voltage only. Real output depends on the load, the module's internal resistance and how much of the concentrated heat reaches the TEG.

gallery.title: Every part, *modelled from scratch*
gallery.intro: I learned SolidWorks for this project and built every part, the assembly and the engineering drawing.
gallery.drawingCaption: Engineering drawing of the full assembly, with orthographic views and a bill of materials.

did.title: What I did
items: Came up with the orbital solar-thermal and TEG concept for the group brief.
Learned SolidWorks from scratch; modelled all ten parts, the assembly and the drawing.
Chose a material for every stage: silver-coated dish, copper receiver and pipes, Bi₂Te₃ TEG, finned aluminium radiator.
Sized the output: 60 couples × 200 μV/K × 100 K gives 1.2 V open circuit.
Designed the group deck and presented the concepts.
Set up the shared Google Docs folder and helped set the technical direction.

improve.title: What I'd improve
items: Size the radiator from a full heat balance, absorbed against radiated, instead of picking the fins by eye.
Model the thermal resistances from receiver to TEG to predict the actual temperature difference, not assume 100 K.
Add a way to keep the dish facing the Sun as the satellite orbits.
Size the battery for the part of each orbit spent in Earth's shadow.
Less text and bigger type; the detail belongs in the delivery.
A shared doc from day one, sprint targets per person, and flagging skill gaps early.
